new_statements.rule_in_words: A blanket statement for the Western Australian Aboriginal languages covered by the handbook: word stress usually falls on the first syllable. Nothing is said about Mangala specifically; the Mangala entry (4.5.2, pp. 160-162) is a bibliographic/handbook entry (names, classification, dialects, speaker numbers, researchers, spelling system, word lists, grammars, materials) with no phonological description at all.
new_statements.exceptions: Only the hedge 'usually'; no exceptions or language-specific deviations named.
new_statements.identity_note: Thieberger 4.5.2 (p. 160) lists the language names/spellings Djuwali, Jiwali, Manala (McKelson), Mangala (Capell), Mangarla (McGregor), Mangunda, Minala, Mungala, Mangai; classification O'Grady, Voegelin and Voegelin (1966) Marrngu, AIATSIS A.65; dialect names per McGregor (1988): Djuwali, Jiwali, Koalgurdi, Yalmbau; location Jurgurra Creek, Edgar Range; under 20 speakers at La Grange and Broome (McGregor 1988). The handbook's stress sentence is not tied to any variety; it is a statement about Western Australian Aboriginal languages in general.

audit.action: a better source should be cited for the same classification
audit.quote_check: confirmed in the copy we hold
audit.reasoning: The classification (fixed-dominant, initial: initial stress) rests on the only reference grammar of the language, a 2020 593-pp PhD grammar by a fieldworker with her own recordings, and the deciding sentence is verbatim at the cited page and section. The file was not yet obtained before; it is now obtained by the project, so the blank strength of the evidence can be raised to held-and-verified. Nothing better exists: Glottolog's remaining entries are a bibliographic handbook, a mis-attached Congo-language grammar, Nyigina/Warrwa notes and McKelson's lesson books, and Agnew's own literature survey cites no phonology article or instrumental study. The description is thin in detail (one sentence, no secondary stress, author flags no prosodic analysis) but that limits refinement (rhythm/secondary stress stay uncoded), not the primary-stress classification, which is also consistent with the Marrngu relatives. works still to obtain

sources.citation: Agnew, Brigitte Louise. 2020. The core of Mangarla grammar. PhD thesis, University of Melbourne. xviii+593 pp. hdl:11343/241927
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.quote: 'Primary stress falls on the first syllable of a word.' Also: long vowels occur mostly 'in the first (stressed) syllable of a word'; 'In unstressed syllables, all three [vowels] can be centred to a neutral [ə]'; clitics 'are unable to bear major stress within the word'; verbalising suffixes 'never take primary word stress'. No secondary-stress or rhythm statement; author notes 'the absence of a detailed prosodic analysis'.
